```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(RdistNN)
```

This advanced guide uses `jackknife_fast_rank()` and its reference
`jackknife_slow_rank()` for a compact-support rank-weighted rule. Applied
users obtain local standard errors directly from their fitted estimators;
see [Getting started](getting-started.html). Statistical conditions and
theory belong to the [paper](https://jakobjuergens.com/research/#orthogonal-inference-conditional-z)
and its references.

## Supply neighbor indices and a signal

For each target, supply the nearest `support + 1` observation indices. The
extra neighbor replaces a deleted member. Here the rule averages the first
three neighbors at each of two targets:

```{r setup-example}
set.seed(4)
n <- 40L
support <- 3L
X <- matrix(rnorm(n * 2), n, 2)
X0 <- rbind(c(0, 0), c(1, 0))
Y <- rnorm(n)

dx <- distance_eval_batch(distance_l2(), X, X0)
ord <- apply(dx, 2L, order)
neighbors <- t(ord[seq_len(support + 1L), , drop = FALSE])
a <- rep(1, support)
phi <- cbind(Y)
```

The argument named `ranks` below contains **observation indices**, with one
row per target. This differs from the `n x m` rank permutations used by
`jackknife_rank_full()`. The compact-support rule is not the exact DNN
weight rule: the unaveraged exact DNN rank table extends to `n-s+k`, rather
than the first `s` observations. Covariate-aware block averaging can extend
nonzero observation weights beyond that rank.

## Compare fast and reference calculations

```{r compare}
fast <- jackknife_fast_rank(ranks = neighbors, a = a, phi = phi)
slow <- jackknife_slow_rank(ranks = neighbors, a = a, phi = phi)
all.equal(fast$theta_loo, slow$theta_loo, tolerance = 1e-12)
```

`theta0` averages the rule across the supplied target rows; it is not a
vector of separate local fits. These rank-only utilities do not identify
duplicate covariate groups. High-level covariate-aware estimators additionally
average duplicate-block weights in the full sample and every deletion, with a
warning that this practical modification is outside the paper's theory.
Deleting a member reduces its block size as well as the reference-sample size;
the survivors use the `n-1` table divided by the remaining block size. The
shared estimator path reuses prefix/postfix deletion sums with a block
correction, rather than rebuilding a weight matrix for each removed row.
See the [worked deletion example](dnn-weights.html#identical-covariate-rows).

Block deletions accumulate the original signals with their actual survivor
weights and retain both parts of each compensated prefix/suffix sum until the
final merge. Averaging a block's signals first can erase a small observation
that survives deletion of a dominant member. Shared origin selection also
accounts for tiny coefficients and nonzero tiny table masses: exceptional
calculations retain the separately rounded raw products before division by
mass. These safeguards use finite double precision and cannot recover mass
already lost in [asymptotic table construction](dnn-weights.html#numerical-limits).

`theta_loo` has one row per deleted reference
observation and one column per signal component.

```{r se}
deleted <- fast$theta_loo[, 1L]
n_ref <- length(deleted)
c(aggregate = fast$theta0,
  standard_error = sqrt((n_ref - 1) / n_ref * sum((deleted - mean(deleted))^2)))
```

Use a numeric `n x q` signal matrix to retain the full reference-sample size.
Function-valued `phi(j, t)` supports target-specific contributions, but the
reference size is then inferred as `max(ranks)`. See `?jackknife_fast_rank`
for the full contract and `?jackknife_rank_full` for full-rank weight tables.
The [notation guide](notation-and-conventions.html) maps the array conventions.
